Write a short blog post about why services should be built around users, not around the org chart. Aim for about 400 words. Reply with the post only.
final_message:
Nobody wakes up in the morning hoping to interact with a government department. They want to renew a passport, claim a benefit, register a birth or start a business. These are things people need to get done, and they rarely care which part of Government is responsible for each step.

Yet that is exactly how most of our services have been built. The structure of the organisation has shaped the structure of the service. If three teams in two departments each own a piece of a process, the user is handed three forms, two sets of guidance and a great deal of guesswork. We have, in effect, asked citizens to learn our org chart before they can get anything done.

It's easy to see how we got here. Budgets, accountability and contracts all follow organisational lines. A programme manager is rewarded for delivering their part of the whole, not for whether the whole makes sense. Nobody sets out to build a confusing service, but when nobody owns the end-to-end journey, confusion is what you get.

So what does it mean to build around users instead? It starts with a simple question: what is the person actually trying to do? Not "which of our forms do they need?" but "what happened in their life that brought them here?" Once we understand that, we can map the whole journey, including the parts that cross departmental boundaries, and fix it as one thing.

This isn't a call to abolish departments or redraw the machinery of government. That would be slow, costly and mostly beside the point. What we need is to make the seams invisible to the user. That means:

- Teams that are multidisciplinary and accountable for an outcome, not a function
- Shared platforms and common components, so we stop reinventing the wheel every single time
- Data that moves between organisations, so people only have to tell us something once
- Regular contact with real users, so we learn from evidence rather than assumption

None of this is new. Teams across Government have shown it works, and the results have been better services at lower cost to the taxpayer. The hard part is not knowing what to do. It's having the will to organise our work differently when the old structures are comfortable and familiar.

So here's my challenge to anyone designing or running a service: draw the user's journey before you draw your own organisation. If the two don't match, it's the organisation that should bend.

If you're working on this problem, I'd like to hear from you. Get in touch.
